title: HITL: Agent self-correction demo (capstone)
description:
## What to build

The capstone demonstration: an AI agent detects a cyclomatic complexity violation via the pre-tool-use hook and self-corrects without human intervention.

Sequence (spec Section 8, Step 3):
1. Task the agent with a feature in graft (Go, block mode) that will naturally cause a CC violation
2. Agent attempts to write the file → pre-tool-use hook fires → calm-bridge blocks with violation message
3. Agent reads the violation message, understands the constraint, and refactors
4. Agent re-attempts the write → hook passes → file written
5. Agent commits → pre-commit hook passes → commit succeeds

This proves the full loop: architectural governance enforced on AI agents at write-time, with the agent treating violations as actionable constraints rather than errors.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Agent tasked with feature that naturally produces CC > threshold
- [ ] Pre-tool-use hook blocks the first write attempt
- [ ] Agent reads violation message from stderr
- [ ] Agent refactors to reduce CC below threshold without human guidance
- [ ] Second write attempt succeeds
- [ ] git commit succeeds (pre-commit hook passes)
- [ ] Entire sequence captured/recorded for demonstration
- [ ] Also demonstrated in C# (block mode, deferred pattern) and Python (advisory mode)

title: AI Slop fitness functions (LDR + DDC)
description:
## What to build

Implement the two AI Slop detection fitness functions from spec Section 5.3:

**Logic Density Ratio (LDR)**: logic_lines / total_lines. Detects hollow, boilerplate-heavy AI-generated code. Logic lines = arithmetic, control flow, state mutation, function calls. Excluded: whitespace, comments, imports, type declarations, structural scaffolding.

**Dependency Discipline Check (DDC)**: used_imports / total_imports. Detects unused imports commonly left by AI agents.

Both are per-file metrics, deterministic, fast, and cross-language.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] LDR calculation implemented for all three languages
- [ ] Logic line classification correct per language (control flow, arithmetic, mutation, calls)
- [ ] DDC calculation implemented for all three languages
- [ ] Import usage detection: each import checked for at least one reference in file body
- [ ] current-architecture.json includes file_metrics (ldr) and import_metrics (ddc) sections
- [ ] governance.json rules for both validated by CALM CLI
- [ ] Violation messages match spec Section 5.3 format (including unused import list for DDC)
- [ ] Unit tests: file with 90% boilerplate triggers LDR violation
- [ ] Unit tests: file with 3/10 imports unused triggers DDC violation

Go LDR now excludes grouped import entries. Python DDC now ignores comments and strings, tracks local bindings by lexical scope, keeps function parameter shadowing local to that function, and treats comprehension targets as local bindings so unused imports cannot evade DDC by name collision.

Rationale:

title: Deep vs. Shallow fitness functions (interface width + implementation depth)
description:
## What to build

Implement the two Deep vs. Shallow fitness functions from spec Section 5.2:

**Rule A — Interface Width Ceiling**: Maximum public methods per CALM node (module/package/namespace). A module with too many public methods imposes high cognitive cost.

**Rule B — Implementation Depth Floor**: Minimum average implementation LOC per public method. Modules with very little logic per public method are likely pass-through facades.

Both rules fire independently per module. Both use data already collected by the analyzers (public method count, LOC).

## What to build

Add the enforcement mode layer to the bridge daemon:

1. Read .calm/config.json from the target repository to determine enforcement-mode (block/advisory/off) and which fitness functions are enabled.
2. Route violations through the mode: block returns status=block with exit 1 intent, advisory returns status=advisory with exit 0 intent, off skips checks entirely.

- [ ] enforcement-mode=off: no analysis performed, returns status=pass

title: Bridge /check endpoint: C# cyclomatic complexity with deferred first-call
description:
## What to build

Wire the full /check endpoint for C# files with the deferred first-call pattern from spec Section 2:

1. First call on a C# file when daemon is cold: return {"status":"pass","warming":true} immediately
2. Daemon warms Roslyn in background, analyzes the file just written
3. If violations found: store in state, keyed by file path
4. On next hook call in same repo: check state for outstanding violations and block

This pattern handles Roslyn's up-to-3s cold start without blocking the first write.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] POST /check with language=csharp on cold daemon returns pass+warming immediately
- [ ] Roslyn analyzer starts in background, analyzes the deferred file
- [ ] Violations stored in state map (repo → file → violations)
- [ ] Subsequent /check calls return block if outstanding violations exist
- [ ] After warm-up, subsequent C# checks are synchronous (no more warming:true)
- [ ] Integration test proving deferred-then-block pattern
- [ ] Integration test proving warm path is synchronous
- [ ] Measured cold start time documented

## Blocked by

- calm-poc-avm (CALM CLI integration)

## Review Skills

When having the work reviewed as prompted, these are the skills to be used for the subagents:

**MUST:**

- golang-error-handling

**SHOULD:**

## Implementation closeout

Implemented the C# /check deferred first-call path. In block mode, the first cold C# request returns pass with warming:true after acquiring the repo serialization lock and starts the deferred Roslyn analysis in the background. The deferred analysis writes proposed content to a temp file, runs the C# analyzer, builds architecture JSON, calls CALM validation, stores violations by repo/file, and marks C# warm only after a successful deferred check. Once warm, C# checks run synchronously. Outstanding C# violations from other files are authoritative on subsequent same-repo hooks; same-file checks may analyze synchronously to clear the violation. Advisory/off modes stay synchronous and clear stale block state consistently with existing behavior.

Added unit coverage for cold deferral, deferred-then-block, warm synchronous block, same-file clearing behavior, existing outstanding block state, advisory stale-state clearing, C# analyzer infrastructure failures, deferred analyzer failure surfacing, recovered deferred panic surfacing, canceled warm-up lock acquisition, and second cold-call serialization. Added tagged integration coverage using the default Roslyn analyzer resolver: cold deferred C# analysis stores a real Render violation, the next file blocks, and a warm same-file clean check clears the violation.

## Subagent review summary

/test-driven-development: Found cold C# bypassed existing outstanding state, cold latency was only logged, and default Roslyn wiring was not covered. Fixed outstanding-state handling, removed flaky hard wall-clock assertion in favor of channel-controlled deferral evidence, and added default Roslyn integration coverage. Final cycle found advisory-mode stale state; fixed by making advisory C# synchronous and clearing stale block state. No third review loop opened because max review cycles is 2; focused and full gates passed after the fix.

/golang-structs-interfaces: Found C# requests while warm-up was already running could return pass,warming without analysis. Fixed by making only the first block-mode cold request deferred; later warming-window requests are serialized through the synchronous path. Final cycle: No findings.

/golang-error-handling: Found deferred warm-up failures were dropped/marked warm and Roslyn failures classified as input. Fixed warm-up failure state, next-call 503 surfacing, Roslyn runner/JSON failure classification as infrastructure, and warm-up failure precedence over outstanding violations. Final cycle found ordering/canceled-lock edge cases; fixed them locally and verified under the two-cycle cap.

/golang-concurrency: Found deferred goroutine could lose the repo-lock race to a second same-repo request. Fixed by acquiring the repo lock before returning pass,warming and handing that held lock to the deferred goroutine. Final cycle found the same pre-return scheduling window; fixed by moving warmupRunning publication after lock acquisition and rechecking state under the lock. No third review loop opened because max review cycles is 2; race/full gates passed after the fix.

/golang-design-patterns: Found outstanding deferred C# violations were not authoritative once C# became warm, and background work lacked daemon lifecycle ownership. Fixed C# outstanding other-file short-circuit, same-file clear path, and handler-owned DeferredContext canceled on /shutdown. Final cycle: No findings.

/golang-testing: Found goroutine tests could hang when helper goroutines called t.Fatalf, the Roslyn integration did not prove next-block/warm-clear behavior, cold latency assertion could flake, and default resolver preferred Debug over ensured Release. Fixed async helper error propagation, expanded integration, removed tight latency threshold, and made default Roslyn resolver prefer Release. Final cycle: No findings.

/golang-safety: Found deferred C# goroutine lacked panic recovery. Fixed recover in startDeferredCheck, recording a warm-up failure and still releasing the repo lock. Final cycle: No findings.

## Conflicts

Conflict:
- The C# deferred-first-call requirement says the first cold request returns pass,warming immediately, while enforcement semantics require the next same-repo hook to block known outstanding violations deterministically.
Decision:
- Defer only the first cold block-mode C# request; before deferral and on every later C# block-mode request, surface warm-up failures first and block if outstanding violations exist in other files. Same-file checks remain allowed so a fix can clear the stored violation.
Rationale:
- This preserves the user-visible cold-start escape hatch without letting deferred violations be masked by unrelated later checks, and keeps the self-correction loop able to fix the original file.

Conflict:
- Returning pass,warming before acquiring the repo lock minimized response work, but allowed scheduler windows where a second request could analyze/pass before the deferred request.
Decision:
- Acquire the repo lock before returning pass,warming, then pass that held lock to the background deferred check.
Rationale:
- The lock acquisition is cheap compared with Roslyn warm-up and gives deterministic deferred-then-block ordering for same-repo hooks.

Conflict:
- Background deferred failures could be dropped because the first request had already returned pass,warming.
Decision:
- Store deferred warm-up failure state, keep C# cold until a successful deferred check, and surface the failure as a 503 before outstanding block state on the next C# block-mode check.
Rationale:
- Silent analyzer failures would undermine the proof of control; surfacing them as infrastructure failures is safer than marking the language warm.

Conflict:
- Advisory mode could either reuse cold C# deferral or run synchronously like Go/Python advisory checks.
Decision:
- Keep C# advisory synchronous and clear stale block state through the existing synchronous mode-routing path.
Rationale:
- Advisory mode is guidance, not a cold-start block path; synchronous routing avoids stale block responses after a mode change.

Conflict:
- Default Roslyn resolver originally preferred Debug, while integration setup ensured Release.
Decision:
- Prefer Release before Debug in the default resolver.
Rationale:
- Tests and runtime defaults now exercise the binary built for stable integration use and avoid stale Debug artifacts.

- Focused default Roslyn integration: TestCheckerWithDefaultRoslynAnalyzerDefersThenBlocksCSharpFixture logged real Roslyn deferred C# cold response latency around 1ms and verified deferred state, next-file block, and warm same-file clear.

When a target repo already has a non-CALM pre-commit hook, install-hooks.sh refuses to install unless CALM_HOOK_OVERWRITE=1 destroys the existing hook. This blocks CALM adoption in repos that already use pre-commit hooks for other tooling.

## What needs to be done

Add CALM_HOOK_APPEND=1 mode that installs CALM as a sidecar hook (.git/hooks/calm-pre-commit) and appends a call block to the existing hook, preserving both.

Changes:
- scripts/install-hooks.sh: new CALM_HOOK_APPEND=1 path + updated idempotency detection
- scripts/install_hooks_test.go: new test cases for append mode
- docs/runbooks/red-green-demo.md: update troubleshooting section with new option

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] CALM_HOOK_APPEND=1 installs sidecar at .git/hooks/calm-pre-commit
- [ ] Existing hook gains a call block with # CALM pre-commit hook (sidecar) marker
- [ ] Re-running with CALM_HOOK_APPEND=1 updates the sidecar, not the existing hook
- [ ] Error message for existing hook mentions CALM_HOOK_APPEND=1 as an option
- [ ] All existing tests still pass
close_reason: CALM_HOOK_APPEND=1 implemented with TDD. Sidecar install, idempotent re-runs, updated error message and runbook. All 6 tests pass.

title: Optimize Python /check synchronous latency below 500ms
description:
## What to build

Investigate and optimize Python `/check` latency so the real synchronous path with radon plus CALM validation consistently stays below the 500ms target from the CALM PoC success criteria.

## Context

During `calm-poc-ldj`, the real integration path passed functionally but measured 521-666ms on repeated runs. The current implementation invokes `radon cc`, `radon raw`, and `calm validate` as separate subprocesses.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Profile Python `/check` subprocess time by phase: temp write, radon cc, radon raw, architecture build, calm validate
- [ ] Reduce or amortize subprocess overhead, or document why 500ms is unrealistic for the PoC architecture
- [ ] Real integration measurement consistently logs <500ms across at least 5 consecutive runs on the target machine
- [ ] Update Beads/docs with the final latency decision

## Discovered from

- calm-poc-ldj review cycle 2 latency conflict
notes:
## Subagent review summary

Cycle 1:
MUST/SHOULD /systematic-debugging: Found single-sample latency logging and missing radon cc/raw phase split. Fixed by adding five-run latency logging and a phase profile that records legacy radon cc, legacy radon raw, Radon API analysis, architecture build, calm validate, and fitness filtering.
MUST/SHOULD /verification-before-completion: Found Beads closure notes missing, five-run evidence absent from the test path, and the final latency decision absent from Beads. Beads notes are added here before closure; docs now include the latency decision.
MUST/SHOULD /golang-testing: Found missing CLI fallback coverage and weak diagnostic profile coverage. Added default-path fallback tests for unavailable fast path and fast-path subprocess failure, real installed-Radon API coverage, five-run integration logging, and legacy-vs-API phase logging.
MUST/SHOULD /golang-code-style: Cycle 1: No findings.

Cycle 2:
MUST/SHOULD /systematic-debugging: Found Beads notes still pending and degraded fast-path fallback coverage missing. Added fallback coverage for a parsed launcher whose fast-path subprocess fails; Beads notes are recorded before closure.
MUST/SHOULD /verification-before-completion: Found Beads notes still pending and older spec wording still said radon subprocess wrapper. Updated spec wording to Radon API subprocess with CLI-compatible fallback; Beads notes are recorded before closure.
MUST/SHOULD /golang-testing: Found integration test did not prove the real Radon API script executes. Added TestAnalyzePythonFileWithRealRadonAPIFastPathWhenAvailable, which invokes analyzePythonFileWithRadonAPI against installed radon.
MUST/SHOULD /golang-code-style: Found long lines and dense assertions. Split fixture paths/log format and extracted assertion booleans in the touched tests.

## Conflict resolution

Conflict: Reviewers requested a hard <500ms assertion across five integration runs, but observed evidence showed the external FINOS CALM Node.js subprocess can occasionally spike above 500ms even after Radon optimization.
Decision: Keep the integration test deterministic by logging five consecutive latency samples and over-budget samples instead of failing normal test runs on wall-clock jitter.
Rationale: The PoC architecture intentionally shells out to FINOS calm validate on the synchronous path. That subprocess dominates latency and is outside Go test control, so a hard wall-clock assertion would be flaky. The spec documents that a hard latency SLO SHOULD be revisited with a long-lived CALM validation service or in-process validator if the PoC moves forward.

Conflict: The task wording asked to profile radon cc and radon raw, but the approved optimization removes those two subprocesses from the default hook path.
Decision: Profile legacy radon cc and radon raw separately for comparison, and profile the optimized Radon API path as the active analysis phase.
Rationale: This preserves the requested root-cause evidence while accurately documenting the new implementation path.

## Latency evidence

Before optimization, five real integration samples were 534.271250ms, 523.878250ms, 523.280625ms, 552.761042ms, and 507.231792ms.
After optimization, five real integration samples were 439.607459ms, 425.79225ms, 432.336625ms, 439.290042ms, and 436.524791ms. A later verification run logged 443.946833ms, 404.831375ms, 406.235875ms, 453.455416ms, and 420.529542ms.
Phase profile from the final run: temp_write=172.875µs, legacy_radon_cc=97.832708ms, legacy_radon_raw=64.522ms, radon_api_analysis=58.739375ms, architecture=376.041µs, calm_validate=362.343375ms, fitness=20.334µs, total=584.338709ms.

## Verification

- go test -count=1 ./internal/analyzer ./internal/bridge: pass
- go test -count=1 -tags=integration -run TestPythonSynchronousCheckPhaseProfile|TestCheckerWithRealCALMBlocksRingstationPythonCyclomaticComplexityFixture -v ./internal/bridge: pass
- go test -count=1 ./...: pass
- go test -race -count=1 ./...: pass

## Final latency decision

The default Python hook path now invokes the Python interpreter from the installed radon launcher once and uses Radon APIs for cyclomatic complexity and raw metrics together. Explicit custom radon paths and fast-path failures retain CLI-compatible radon cc/raw fallback. The 500ms target is met in the recorded target-machine five-run samples, while the spec documents that occasional external CALM CLI jitter can exceed the budget and should be addressed with a long-lived validator if this becomes a production SLO. No findings remain unresolved after two review cycles.
close_reason: Completed Python /check latency optimization, docs, review resolution, and verification evidence

title: Improve C# Dependency Discipline with project-aware import resolution
description:
## What to build

Upgrade the C# analyzer so Dependency Discipline can enforce meaningful thresholds instead of the current advisory/no-op `gte 0` baseline. The analyzer should load enough project compilation context for project-local namespaces and references, then recompute C# DDC baselines and propose a non-zero threshold.

## Context

During `calm-poc-d2g`, Peter explicitly approved the temporary Dependency Discipline threshold of `0` for the PoC only if project-aware C# import resolution is tracked as follow-up work. Current single-file Roslyn analysis resolves platform namespaces and aliases but cannot reliably resolve every project-local namespace import.

## Acceptance criteria

- C# analyzer accepts project or solution context when available
- Project-local namespace imports are resolved accurately enough for DDC calibration
- Unit/integration tests cover project-local namespace usage and unused imports
- SlackStatus and StackOverflow.Api.V3 baseline reports are regenerated
- `patterns/governance.json` is updated or a calibration recommendation is documented with a non-zero DDC threshold
- Review notes include findings from `/dotnet-backend-patterns`, `/golang-error-handling`, and `/test-driven-development`


## Required Skills
dotnet-backend-patterns,golang-error-handling,test-driven-development
